routes.description: Establish theism as a legitimate personal explanation whose simplicity and divine purposes make the universe's order, consciousness, moral agency, and associated general features more probable than they would be without God.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it supplies a coherent personal-explanation framework, connects simplicity to prior probability, derives relevant expectations from the proposed divine nature, and accounts for apparent counterevidence without losing the comparative explanatory inference.

motionBridge.description: Show that a simple divine-agent hypothesis makes the universe and its general features sufficiently more expected than relevant non-theistic alternatives to count as the most probable explanation.

centralBridges.description: Establish purposive personal causation as a genuine and applicable explanatory mode alongside explanation through physical states and laws.
Justify simplicity as a basis for assigning prior probability while retaining evidential fit and predictive accuracy as constraints on hypothesis choice.
Derive reasons for a perfectly good and powerful God to create an orderly, life-producing universe containing conscious agents with consequential freedom.
Reconcile grave suffering and other apparent tensions with the proposed divine nature through morally relevant opportunity, obligations toward sufferers, or compensating goods.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Specify how economy in entities, properties, and mathematical structure operates in ordinary explanatory and scientific comparisons.
Connect regular natural laws and embodied conditions to the possibility of rational consciousness, purposive action, and morally significant choice.

routes.description: Deny that the proposed divine hypothesis earns the claimed comparative probability by challenging its explanatory category, simplicity, predictive specificity, coherence, and ability to accommodate suffering and human nature.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if one or more indispensable links from divine simplicity to explanatory probability fails, or if the hypothesis remains insufficiently discriminating, internally strained, or poorly aligned with major features it is offered to explain.

motionBridge.description: Show that the available general features do not warrant treating God as the simplest and most probable explanation because the proposed comparison lacks a justified or adequately predictive basis.

centralBridges.description: Challenge the exhaustiveness or applicability of the division between inanimate causal explanation and purposive personal explanation.
Show that competing notions of simplicity can diverge and that an infinite, qualified divine agent may not be simple in the sense relevant to probability.
Require theism to provide discriminating expectations rather than unrestricted compatibility with possible observations or merely general explanatory coverage.
Test whether the extent and distribution of severe suffering are compatible with the purposes and obligations attributed to a perfectly good and omnipotent creator.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require the proposed personal cause to address its fit with established causal knowledge, evolutionary explanation, and physical accounts of space and time.
Examine whether an independently created immaterial component coheres with evolutionary development, embodied cognition, and the biological cost of the human brain.

sections.title: Personal, physical, and purposive explanation
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether divine agency belongs to a defensible explanatory category and whether the proposed contrast with physical causation is sufficiently complete to support the wider inference.

sections.title: Simplicity as a guide to explanatory probability
sections.rationale: The motion expressly links simplicity with probability, making the meaning, justification, and limits of simplicity central to the comparison between theism and alternative hypotheses.

sections.title: Predicting order, life, consciousness, and agency
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether the proposed divine nature generates substantive expectations for the universe's general features and whether those expectations distinguish theism from rival accounts.

sections.title: Divine attributes, physical coherence, and human nature
sections.rationale: Questions about temporality, knowledge, unlimited power, souls, evolution, and embodiment bear on whether the explanatory hypothesis is coherent and appropriately connected to the phenomena invoked.

sections.title: Suffering, moral freedom, and posthumous compensation
sections.rationale: Severe and unevenly distributed suffering is major apparent counterevidence to a perfectly good creator, while freedom, victim benefit, and compensation supply the corresponding reconciliatory requirements.

moves.speaker: Richard Swinburne
moves.proposition: Personal explanation through an animate agent's purposes, beliefs, and powers is a genuine explanatory mode alongside explanation by prior physical states and natural laws.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage is a continuous portion of Swinburne's opening speech and uses his explicit first-person terminology and example.

response.rationale: Constructive move establishing personal explanation as an explanatory category; no earlier opposing target applies.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: A clear constructive foundation within its class, though its applicability beyond familiar agents remains undeveloped.

precisionFindings.rationale: The explanatory category is stated through purposes, beliefs, and powers and contrasted clearly with physical explanation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move claims a genuine explanatory mode and supports that bounded claim with an ordinary agency example.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction is internally consistent and supported by a recognizable action-explanation example; broader applicability is only implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The hand-action example supports the existence of personal explanation, but does not independently establish cosmic applicability.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Directly supplies the indispensable personal-causation bridge at the top of the central tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: No meaningful opposing alternative is interpreted in this constructive span.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly defines personal explanation by an animate being's purposes, beliefs, and powers and contrasts it with Newtonian explanation.

moves.speaker: Richard Swinburne
moves.proposition: Explanatory practice favors hypotheses that posit fewer entities, properties, laws, and mathematical complications, as illustrated by ordinary and scientific comparisons among otherwise viable explanations.
moves.attributionBasis: This uninterrupted argument remains within Swinburne's opening address and develops his own stated definition and scientific examples.

response.rationale: Constructive move defining economy across entities, properties, laws, and mathematical form; no earlier opposing target applies.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It gives a substantive simplicity principle and scientific illustration, with the probability bridge compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The dimensions of simplicity are recoverable, though their aggregation into a single comparative measure remains implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Scientific preference supports simplicity as a consideration, but the step from preference to prior probability is compressed.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The examples illustrate economy, but the bridge from several simplicity dimensions to a unified probability ordering remains material.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Scientific examples provide relevant support while leaving rival simplicity measures and evidential fit undercompared.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Directly addresses the central simplicity-inference requirement and is highly placed within that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The constructive span does not materially interpret an opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt presents Newtonian gravitation as simple by scientific standards against indefinitely many more complicated alternatives.

moves.speaker: Richard Swinburne
moves.proposition: A perfectly good and omnipotent God has reason to create rational conscious beings able to make serious, consequential choices between good and evil rather than beings programmed only to do good.
moves.attributionBasis: Swinburne explicitly labels this as his hypothesis and develops the divine attributes and creative rationale in one continuous passage.

response.rationale: Constructive move deriving a creative reason from perfect goodness and the value of serious free choice; no earlier target applies.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It develops a central divine-purpose expectation, while the moral necessity of consequential evil remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim and key terms are clear, but the required extent and distribution of evil are not scoped.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The value of unprogrammed choice supplies a reason, but not by itself the stronger distributional expectation implied.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from valuable serious choice to alternatives between good and evil is coherent, with a bounded unstated proportionality bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The account is principally a moral-purpose assertion and does not compare alternative ways God might secure meaningful agency.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies a central reason for divine creation of consequentially free rational agents.

representationalCharity.rationale: No opposing interpretation is materially assessed in this constructive move.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that God would prefer chosen goodness over programmed goodness and therefore permit serious choices affecting the world and others.

moves.speaker: Richard Swinburne
moves.proposition: Theism makes an orderly, life-producing universe containing conscious embodied agents probable because regular laws enable agency and evolution, whereas physics alone does not explain why conscious beings exist.
moves.attributionBasis: The extended first-person argument occurs wholly within Swinburne's opening speech and culminates in his explicit comparative probability conclusion.

response.rationale: Constructive comparative move linking divine purposes to laws, evolution, consciousness, and probability; no earlier opposing target applies.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It reaches the motion-level comparison, though relevant non-theistic alternatives receive limited treatment.

precisionFindings.rationale: The prediction is recoverable, but the universal claim about physics and the relevant comparison class lack explicit scope limits.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The divine-purpose reasoning is relevant, but the categorical dismissal of physical explanation and resulting probability claim exceed the supplied comparison.

charity.alternative: Physical and evolutionary accounts may explain order and embodiment while leaving consciousness partly unresolved.
charity.decisiveQualification: A residual explanatory gap does not alone show that theism makes the entire package most probable.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The sequence from divine purposes to useful laws and agents is intelligible, but the comparative-probability conclusion needs an explicit rival and likelihood bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move relies substantially on asserted divine intentions and a categorical claim about physics without representative alternative comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the motion bridge by asserting comparative probability for the universe's central general features.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move acknowledges evolution but materially underdevelops the strongest non-theistic division of explanatory labor.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says God produces agents through evolutionary laws, denies that physics can explain consciousness without many categories, and draws a comparative probability conclusion.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Purposive behavior in evolved organisms and algorithmic systems shows that explanation is not exhaustively divided between mechanical processes and personal agents.
moves.attributionBasis: Millican has been formally introduced and explicitly identifies Richard's two explanatory kinds before presenting his objections and examples.

components.text: Whether the proposed contrast exhausts the available explanatory modes for purposive behavior.

response.rationale: It expressly diagnoses the proposed mechanical-or-personal division as non-exhaustive and gives algorithmic and evolutionary purposiveness as counterclasses.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The decisive exhaustiveness inference is explicitly identified and challenged with two concrete counterexamples.

precisionFindings.rationale: The counterclaim is clear, though 'purposive' shifts somewhat between function-like behavior and an agent's conscious purpose.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion is limited to rejecting exhaustiveness, and the speaker notes that Swinburne may accept part of the distinction.

charity.alternative: Swinburne's category concerns causal explanation by conscious purposes, not every system displaying function-like purposiveness.
charity.decisiveQualification: Algorithmic and evolved behavior defeats exhaustiveness only if it constitutes an additional causal explanatory mode rather than physical explanation at another level.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The examples undermine a simple exhaustive dichotomy, though the equivocation between conscious purpose and functional purposiveness weakens the defeat.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Algorithms and evolved organisms are specific relevant cases, but their status as genuinely distinct causal modes is not fully defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Directly supports the central challenge to the explanatory framework's exhaustiveness.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection is fair to an exhaustive formulation but does not fully preserve the narrower conscious-purpose distinction.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes chess algorithms, animals, plants, and evolutionary logic before expressly calling the mechanical-or-personal division incorrect.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Simplicity is not a unitary guide to probability because descriptive, ontological, and computational simplicity can diverge, while scientific progress sometimes favors more complex hypotheses.
moves.attributionBasis: Millican expressly attributes the emphasis on simplicity to Richard and then supplies a sustained historical and conceptual criticism.

components.text: Whether simplicity supplies a unitary ordering when descriptive, ontological, and computational measures diverge.
Whether scientific movement toward more complex but better-fitting theories limits the stated simplicity preference.

response.rationale: It identifies two failures in an unrestricted simplicity inference: multiple non-equivalent criteria and historical cases where complexity increases.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Both decisive qualifications to the initial simplicity principle are expressly contacted, although no replacement aggregation rule is offered.

precisionFindings.rationale: Distinct simplicity criteria and the restricted historical claim are clearly separated and scoped.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The examples support the bounded conclusion that simplicity is multifaceted and not invariably preferred.

charity.alternative: Simplicity can remain one probabilistic virtue while predictive fit determines which adequate hypotheses are compared.
charity.decisiveQualification: Divergent measures still require an account of which simplicity notion is probabilistically relevant.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The divergence of criteria and the possibility of warranted complexity form a consistent, directly relevant limitation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Conceptual distinctions and scientific history provide specific support, with the exact prevalence and aggregation issue left open.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It reaches the indispensable central adequacy question for simplicity at the top of its tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection preserves simplicity as a possible conditional virtue while exposing the missing selection rule.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that science sometimes moves to more complex hypotheses and distinguishes descriptive from ontological simplicity.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Bodiless instantaneous agency is unlike observed causation, and scientific history's retreat from intuitive purposive explanations makes background fit relevant even to a cosmic hypothesis.
moves.attributionBasis: Millican directly reconstructs Richard's background-knowledge position and follows it with an extended objection grounded in experience and scientific history.

components.text: Whether familiar personal explanation provides relevant background support for bodiless instantaneous cosmic agency.

response.rationale: The move directly contests extension from observed embodied agency to the proposed cosmic cause by invoking causal experience and scientific history.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the applicability demand clearly, though the selected evidence emphasizes history more than the precise bodiless-agency comparison.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is bounded to background fit and the historical retreat from particular purposive explanations.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The material supports treating background fit as relevant without claiming that unfamiliar causation is impossible.

charity.alternative: Cosmic explanations concern a unique domain where ordinary causal background may have limited authority.
charity.decisiveQualification: Domain uniqueness does not make background fit irrelevant; it changes how strongly the mismatch counts.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from scientific retreat and observed causation to a background-fit concern is coherent but not decisive against a unique cause.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Historical examples are specific and relevant, while the leap to bodiless instantaneous agency is supported mainly by analogy.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly occupies the subsidiary background-fit tier but does not itself decide the central existence of personal explanation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection fairly preserves the possible uniqueness defense while challenging the stronger dismissal of background fit.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt rejects indifference to background knowledge and cites scientific abandonment of Aristotelian purposive accounts of falling bodies and planetary motion.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: An unrestricted creator hypothesis can be verbally simple yet explanatorily non-specific, while observed natural purposiveness is explained through Darwinian evolution operating with physical mechanisms.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage remains in Millican's uninterrupted response and presents an explicit parody followed by his observation about natural purposiveness.

components.text: Whether a simple creator hypothesis supplies discriminating expectations rather than accommodating any observed outcome by an unspecified desire.
Whether verbal brevity can count as explanatory simplicity when it purchases no predictive specificity.

response.rationale: The cup-of-water example expressly diagnoses unrestricted creator preference as simple in words but explanatorily hopeless because non-specific.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly identifies the missing predictive restriction and states why verbal simplicity cannot repair it.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between verbal simplicity and explanatory specificity is clear and consistently maintained.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The counterexample warrants the bounded conclusion that unrestricted intentions yield weak prediction.

charity.alternative: A creator's perfect goodness may constrain intentions enough to generate substantive expectations.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those moral constraints must be independently specified and shown to discriminate among possible worlds.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counterexample cleanly shows that concise intentional attribution alone does not yield discriminating explanatory content.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The illustrative case strongly supports the conceptual point, though it does not quantify how constrained the actual theistic hypothesis is.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central predictive-content bridge at the top of that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection leaves room for constrained divine purposes while correctly requiring those constraints to do predictive work.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls a creator-desire explanation very simple but hopelessly non-specific and contrasts it with Darwinian purposiveness working with physical mechanisms.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: An infinite divine agent is not straightforwardly simple because its powers have qualifications concerning evil and future free actions, and sustaining every particle implies immense computational capacity.
moves.attributionBasis: The move occurs within Millican's uninterrupted opening rebuttal turn and explicitly addresses Swinburne's account of divine infinity.

components.text: Whether an infinite divine agent is simple under the relevant ontological, descriptive, and computational criteria.
Whether qualifications concerning evil and future free actions complicate the proposed divine attributes.

response.rationale: It directly applies multiple simplicity criteria to the proposed God and identifies qualifications and computational demands that complicate the hypothesis.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It squarely contacts divine simplicity, with some claims about computational burden remaining analogical.

precisionFindings.rationale: The several complexity challenges are recoverable, though computational complexity is applied to an agent without a fully specified metric.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker presents the computational point as a suggestion and supports the attribute qualifications directly.

charity.alternative: Infinite power may be specified by one simple unbounded property, with moral inability and free-action ignorance following from independent principles.
charity.decisiveQualification: The simplicity claim must count the qualifying principles and distinguish concise specification from implementation cost.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The challenge coherently separates qualified scope and computational demand, though sustaining particles does not by itself prove descriptive complexity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The stated doctrinal qualifications are specific; the immense computational-capacity inference lacks a defended complexity model.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Directly supports the central simplicity-adequacy challenge to the divine hypothesis.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes the simple-infinity rationale implicitly but fairly presses the qualifications and competing metric.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt points to limitations regarding evil and future free actions and to the task of maintaining every particle moment by moment.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: A temporal God who knows everything up to a universal present but not future free actions appears incompatible with general relativity's denial of absolute simultaneity.
moves.attributionBasis: The challenge is delivered continuously by Millican during his rebuttal and directly names the commitments he attributes to Swinburne.

components.text: Whether a temporal omniscient God can distinguish a universal present from future free actions under relativity.

response.rationale: It identifies the alleged incompatibility between a universal divine time boundary and relativity's denial of absolute simultaneity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The coherence issue is explicit, though the earlier selected move does not itself fully state the temporal-omniscience theory being attacked.

precisionFindings.rationale: The challenge specifies temporal knowledge, future free actions, and relative simultaneity without material drift.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The wording presents an apparent incompatibility rather than claiming a demonstrated logical contradiction.

charity.alternative: Divine knowledge might be indexed to a relativistic foliation, proper time, or tenseless spacetime rather than an absolute cosmic present.
charity.decisiveQualification: Such a model must preserve the asserted temporal boundary on foreknowledge without reintroducing privileged simultaneity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Relative simultaneity creates a clear tension for a universal present, although incompatibility depends on the exact divine-time model.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: General relativity supplies a specific established premise; the attributed temporal model is not developed enough here to close all reconciliations.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It is a strong subsidiary background-fit and coherence challenge rather than direct motion completion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection is fair but leaves several sophisticated reconciliation models unexamined.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes relativity of simultaneity against God's knowing all events up to time T while lacking knowledge of later free actions.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: A freedom-based justification does not explain severe suffering and early death that deprive infants and other victims of opportunities to exercise morally significant agency.
moves.attributionBasis: Millican explicitly directs this objection to Swinburne near the end of his uninterrupted opening rebuttal turn.

components.text: Whether grave suffering is justified by agency when many victims are deprived of meaningful agency by suffering or early death.

response.rationale: It identifies an internal mismatch in the freedom rationale: some severe harms remove the very opportunity offered as their justification.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The decisive moral-purpose inference is explicitly contacted with concrete counterexamples and a clear defeating consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The objection is specifically limited to victims whose suffering or death prevents meaningful moral action.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move says these cases are hard to explain rather than claiming that all freedom-based defenses are impossible.

charity.alternative: Other agents' freedom, collective goods, or posthumous life might provide benefits not exercised by the immediate victim on Earth.
charity.decisiveQualification: A perfectly good creator still needs a victim-centered justification for allowing deprivation of that person's agency.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counterexample exposes a direct tension between valuing morally significant opportunity and permitting conditions that eliminate it.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Infant starvation and exterminated children are specific representative cases; the remaining gap concerns possible additional justifications.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the central moral-evidence challenge at the top of the tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The challenge fairly targets the stated agency rationale while leaving other possible defenses open.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts the claimed good of morally significant power with infants who starve and victims exterminated before exercising such power.

moves.speaker: Richard Swinburne
moves.proposition: Purposiveness in causal explanation requires a purposive agent: biological functions can be explained through selection, while ordinary goal-directed action exemplifies irreducibly personal causation.
moves.attributionBasis: The move begins with Swinburne's answer to Millican and continues within Swinburne's clearly bounded rebuttal turn.

components.text: Whether evolved functions and algorithms constitute a third causal explanatory category beyond physical and personal explanation.

response.rationale: The reply distinguishes selection-based biological function from purposive action and reasserts beliefs, plans, and powers as personal causation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the central counterexample and supplies a distinction, though it does not fully analyze algorithmic systems.

precisionFindings.rationale: The personal category is clear, but the universal claim that no other causal-explanation kinds exist is broader than the developed defense.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Ordinary planning supports personal explanation but only partially warrants the exhaustive categorical conclusion.

charity.alternative: Algorithmic and evolutionary explanations may be physically realized yet explanatory at autonomous functional levels.
charity.decisiveQualification: Multiple explanatory levels do not necessarily create a distinct fundamental causal mode.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The selection-versus-conscious-purpose distinction is coherent, while the final exhaustiveness claim retains an unstated exclusion argument.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Ordinary planning and biological selection are relevant cases, but algorithms and higher-level functional explanation are incompletely compared.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the con side's central explanatory-framework bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly absorbs evolutionary function into selection but gives the algorithmic autonomy alternative limited attention.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes plans, purposes, beliefs about consequences, and powers as explanations of ordinary action and concludes against additional causal kinds.

moves.speaker: Richard Swinburne
moves.proposition: Among hypotheses that adequately fit the evidence, greater simplicity raises prior probability, although even a simple hypothesis must be rejected when its predictions conflict with the data.
moves.attributionBasis: Swinburne develops the point throughout his uninterrupted rebuttal turn while directly answering Millican's scientific counterexamples.

components.text: Whether scientific acceptance of more complex theories defeats simplicity as a probability guide.
Whether simplicity operates only after predictive adequacy and evidential fit are held suitably fixed.

response.rationale: It concedes movement to more complex laws when predictions improve and restricts simplicity preference to hypotheses satisfying the evidence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly answers the scientific-complexity counterexample and states the decisive evidential-fit qualification.

precisionFindings.rationale: The domain of the simplicity preference is expressly restricted to hypotheses with adequate evidential satisfaction.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The Boyle–Charles and van der Waals comparison appropriately supports the conditional rather than absolute simplicity claim.

charity.alternative: Multiple simplicity measures can still diverge even among equally accurate hypotheses.
charity.decisiveQualification: The response repairs the fit objection but does not specify which simplicity measure determines the remaining prior ordering.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional principle is coherent and resolves the apparent conflict with more accurate complex theories; metric choice remains open.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A specific scientific replacement illustrates why accuracy can outweigh simplicity, with the probabilistic principle itself only briefly defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central simplicity-adequacy challenge and restores a qualified inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: It handles the strongest predictive-fit objection but leaves the multifaceted-simplicity component substantially unanswered.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explains replacement of the simpler Boyle–Charles law by the more accurate van der Waals law, then limits simplicity preference to adequately supported hypotheses.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Theism's generality yields too little precision to share the evidential standing of scientific hypotheses whose unfamiliarity or complexity is justified by accurate, discriminating predictions.
moves.attributionBasis: The move is delivered by Millican after the floor changes to him and explicitly follows up Swinburne's preceding account of simplicity.

components.text: Whether theism meets the response's evidential-fit condition through precise and discriminating predictions.
Whether simplicity often trades against specificity, making a concise hypothesis evidentially weak.

response.rationale: The reply accepts simplicity between equally precise rivals but argues that theism lacks the precision that lets complex scientific theories earn evidential support.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly targets the qualified simplicity rule at its evidential-fit premise and states the consequence for theism.

precisionFindings.rationale: Precision, specificity, accuracy, and equal scope are distinguished consistently and the comparison is expressly conditional.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim is calibrated to an evidential disadvantage rather than an assertion that general hypotheses are never explanatory.

charity.alternative: Theism may predict broad classes of phenomena probabilistically without numerical precision.
charity.decisiveQualification: Broad expectations still need likelihood contrast with relevant alternatives to carry comparative evidential weight.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between equal-fit simplicity comparisons and theism's alleged lack of specificity directly follows from the conceded principle.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Scientific prediction provides a concrete comparison, though the exact predictive content of theism is characterized more than exhaustively demonstrated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central predictive-content requirement at the top of its tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply allows simplicity to decide equally predictive cases and focuses fairly on the missing discriminating content.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt concedes preference for simpler laws when precision, accuracy, and scope are equal, then stresses that simplicity commonly reduces specificity and contrasts this with precise scientific predictions.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: A separately created immaterial soul fits poorly with a long evolutionary history and the development of a resource-intensive human brain if the soul itself performs human thinking.
moves.attributionBasis: The argument remains in Millican's continuous turn and identifies Swinburne's soul theory before drawing its evolutionary consequences.

components.text: Whether the proposed account of consciousness coheres with evolutionary history and the explanatory role of the physical brain.

response.rationale: It directly demands an account of why costly evolved brains are needed if an independently inserted immaterial soul performs the thinking.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The evolutionary-fit demand is clear and concrete, although the selected pro move does not fully articulate the soul theory challenged.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional criticism clearly identifies separate soul creation, thinking, brain cost, and evolutionary development.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move asks for a missing fit story rather than claiming evolution logically excludes an immaterial soul.

charity.alternative: The brain may mediate sensory input, action, development, or soul-body interaction even if the soul is the subject of thought.
charity.decisiveQualification: The theory must explain why those functions require the observed scale and evolutionary cost of the brain.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Given the attributed premise that the soul does the thinking, the demand to explain the brain's costly evolution follows clearly.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Evolutionary duration and large brains are specific relevant facts, though the exact soul-body division of labor is not documented in this span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly occupies the subsidiary human-nature bridge without directly resolving the broader motion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection fairly frames a demand for integration rather than treating evolution as a simple contradiction.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts 13.8 billion years of physical development with divine insertion of a soul and asks why enormous brains evolved if the soul can think.

moves.speaker: Richard Swinburne
moves.proposition: God's omnipotence permits posthumous compensation, and God's obligation as creator requires giving sufferers an afterlife when necessary to ensure that each person's total life is good overall.
moves.attributionBasis: Swinburne advances the argument in his concluding response, with the speaker turn remaining continuous until Millican resumes.

components.text: Whether victims whose earthly lives are gravely bad can receive a victim-centered good sufficient to answer the moral objection.

response.rationale: The reply directly proposes an afterlife, grounded in omnipotence and creator obligation, to make each sufferer's total life good overall.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the victim-centered demand directly, but does not yet explain how compensation relates to lost agency or development.

precisionFindings.rationale: The condition requiring an afterlife and the total-life conception of compensation are expressly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Omnipotence supports ability, but the claimed creator obligation and adequacy of total-life compensation require additional moral argument.

charity.alternative: Some harms involve non-fungible lost opportunities that later welfare cannot replace.
charity.decisiveQualification: Making a total life good overall does not by itself show that permitting each severe earthly deprivation was morally permissible.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Ability, obligation, and total-life goodness form a usable line, but ability does not entail obligation and compensation does not alone justify permission.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The afterlife and obligation are asserted theological-moral premises without independent support or comparison to non-compensable loss.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central moral-evidence bridge through a proposed victim-centered reconciliation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply addresses victim benefit but compresses the strongest non-compensability and permission-versus-reparation distinction.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says omnipotence enables life after death and creator obligation requires it where necessary so that the person's total life is good.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Posthumous compensation neither follows from a terrible earthly life nor restores the lost embodied opportunity of children killed prematurely to develop moral character.
moves.attributionBasis: Millican begins a new and clearly attributed turn by identifying Swinburne's immediately preceding life-after-death response as his target.

components.text: Whether later compensation can restore the embodied opportunity for moral development lost through premature suffering and death.
Whether a terrible earthly life itself supplies a warrant for the asserted posthumous compensation.

response.rationale: It distinguishes later welfare from restoration of a lost developmental opportunity and states why total-life compensation does not answer that deprivation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The decisive adequacy inference is explicitly identified, challenged, and tied to the concrete case of children denied character development.

precisionFindings.rationale: The reply precisely distinguishes compensation, worthwhile life, and irretrievable embodied moral development.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The irreversibility point is strong, though saying posthumous repair is logically impossible goes beyond what the brief argument establishes.

charity.alternative: An afterlife might include continued development and goods sufficient to make the whole life worthwhile.
charity.decisiveQualification: Continued development would not retroactively supply the particular earthly opportunity or automatically justify its deprivation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between later benefit and restoration of a lost opportunity is coherent; strict logical impossibility remains underargued.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The cases of starving or murdered children concretely support the developmental-loss claim, while impossibility of all posthumous redress is not established.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central moral-evidence bridge by attacking the principal compensation reply.
